events.Japan: Gilbert heavy/photo missions, traffic analysis and known US assault training sustain HIGH probability of a new Central-Pacific offensive, but Marshalls are only one of several plausible objective sets.
events.US: Kwajalein/Roi-Namur + Majuro direct option becomes the operational centerline; outer-island-first remains contingency rather than main plan.

events.Japan: Submarine status reports, increased oiler/transport traffic and US reconnaissance move Marshalls to MEDIUM-HIGH likely objective. Air dispersal, radar/plot readiness, night repair and final construction priorities are raised.
events.carrier_effect: Four first-line Japanese carriers enter radio-disciplined forward holding posture; secondary carriers remain rear-deck reserve.

events.Japan: Outer submarines obtain repeated logistics/escort cues. Kwajalein/Roi becomes the leading but not certain target. Search arcs are narrowed; useful long-range searches rise to roughly 8-10/day plus 2-3 confirmation sorties when weather permits.
events.US: Assault/support echelons continue approach under EMCON and weather masking. Extra Tarawa-derived fire support does not erase oiler, ASW or deck-cycle constraints.

events.Japan: One or more support/assault contacts confirm a major amphibious operation and make Kwajalein/Roi HIGH-likelihood. Carrier centroid remains unknown. No Japanese carrier GO.
events.note: Radar contributes local warning and sortie preservation; the oceanic approach cue still comes mainly from submarines, DF/traffic and aircraft.

events.Japan: A Taroa-centered long-range search aircraft, sent down a submarine/traffic-cued corridor, visually acquires one US fast-carrier TG roughly 330-410 nmi S/SSW of Maloelap/Taroa. At least two flight decks, heavy escorts and many destroyers are reported before CAP drives the scout off.
events.confidence: HIGH one fast-carrier TG; MEDIUM-HIGH larger multi-TG operation; total deck count unresolved.
events.US_effect: The scout's appearance/drive-off makes tactical compromise likely. Course and local CAP/ASW posture are adjusted; operation is not aborted.

events.Japan: An inner submarine obtains a strong hydrophone/brief-visual recontact on the moving corridor. Position uncertainty remains roughly 15-25 nmi; enough for a limited land-based night opportunity but not a Japanese carrier mass strike solution.
events.action: A bounded 8-10 aircraft G4M-class night torpedo package is released from the already-counted Marshall attack pool.
events.result: US radar pickets, night CAP, maneuver and squalls defeat the attack. Centerline: no US ship hit; 3-5 Japanese aircraft irrecoverable. Opportunity is real; success is not awarded automatically.

events.Japan: Additional submarine/air reports confirm at least a second major carrier/support axis and the amphibious character of the operation, but there is no continuous all-TF58 track. The four-carrier force closes eastward conditionally and prepares dawn packages; launch remains withheld.
events.US: Tactical surprise is considered compromised. First major suppression is biased to the earliest fuel/weather-feasible edge of the 1-2 Feb window rather than waiting passively.

state_at_31JanT24.Japanese_knowledge: HIGH major Marshall assault and one or more fast-carrier groups; HIGH Kwajalein/Roi as leading target; incomplete total TF58 geometry.
state_at_31JanT24.Japanese_land_air: About high-130s/low-140s combat-serviceable after routine attrition and the failed night package; aircraft remain dispersed among multiple runway and water-air nodes.
state_at_31JanT24.Japanese_carriers: Four first-line decks conditional-GO prepared, no launch; secondary four decks remain rear support.
state_at_31JanT24.US: 11 fast decks combat operational, tactical surprise degraded but operational initiative retained; first suppression expected 1-2 Feb.
state_at_31JanT24.next_gate: Resolve first US suppression cycle against the newly hardened/sensor-networked Marshall system while simultaneously checking whether Japanese submarine/water-air recontact can create a four-carrier dawn-strike gate.
